reviewIndex.institution: University of Amsterdam and Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam

audience.programmeDescription: Ancient Studies is a joint UvA–VU degree combining the history, texts, objects and ideas of the ancient Mediterranean and Near East. Students study cultural interaction and the later uses of antiquity, then complete a specialisation and interdisciplinary thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The UCR options connect archaeology, ancient democracy, literature, myth and philosophy with historical and cultural interpretation. The joint degree offers a more sustained ancient-world curriculum, a required specialisation and an excursion. This comparison uses its English-taught Ancient History route.

componentNotes.y1-01: The Academic Literacy Test, ACASA orientation and tutoring support carry no credits. Writing support is provided when the diagnostic test indicates it is needed.
componentNotes.y1-seminar: This orientation seminar follows the two first-year cultural-history surveys and prepares for Ancient History. Seminar participation is compulsory.
componentNotes.y2-01: Entry requires both first-year Cultural History of the Ancient World courses, or equivalent introductory study.
componentNotes.y2-04: Students prepare and carry out an interdisciplinary excursion research project. Practical exercises require at least 85% attendance under the programme regulations.
componentNotes.y3-02: The 30 EC elective period may include a minor, approved study abroad or a placement of up to 12 EC. Normally no more than 12 EC may be introductory, and at least 24 EC must be outside the programme. Approved exceptions apply to specified minors and language sequences.
componentNotes.y3-04: The 12 EC thesis includes the thesis colloquium. Students must pass all first- and second-year courses before starting. They conduct individual interdisciplinary research under supervision.

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.text: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.

GOSGATE102.name: Law, Society & Justice
GOSGATE102.text: Law, Society & Justice examines legal, social and normative perspectives on law. Students compare legal traditions and study public and private law, human rights, justice, social control and change, race and gender. Case briefs, demand letters and mock trials develop legal reasoning, while a family-law topic supports the design of a socio-legal research proposal.

GOSHIST111.text: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.

GOSHIST211.text: History of Empires examines empires across global history and competing theories of empire. Students study expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. Historical cases, source analysis and an independent research essay connect theoretical interpretation with specific imperial experiences.

GOSHIST213.text: Provides a chronological overview of warfare in the Western world from antiquity to the present. Covers weapons, technology, strategy, defence, mercenaries, cavalry, chivalry, Blitzkrieg, guerrilla warfare and nuclear arsenals, illustrating competition for mastery in Western history.

GOSHIST311.text: Native American Histories studies Indigenous social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, reciprocity and relational accountability guide collaboration with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders through arts-based work and a public-history project.

MCCHEAM315.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
MCCHEAM315.text:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century.


Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants.


This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.text: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.
